title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across US airspace
content:
The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment.
“After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.
The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about “weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics” to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft.
However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency.

report.summary: FAA expands its $875 million AI advisory system SMART nationwide after a D.C. pilot cut delays and fuel use, though the controllers’ union says it was sidelined.
report.background: US airspace is congested and weather-sensitive, and the FAA has been under pressure to modernize aging traffic-management tools while reducing delays and fuel burn. The agency piloted SMART in National Capital Region airspace from September 21, then said on November 10 it would extend the cloud-based advisory tool to all 22 air route traffic control centers. The $875 million system fits a broader push to add AI decision support to aviation, but it also lands in a sensitive labor environment: airline executives back the rollout, while the union representing controllers says it was not involved in design or testing. The FAA stresses that human specialists in Washington validate every recommendation before it reaches controllers, framing SMART as advice rather than automated control. The expansion will test whether a localized pilot’s reported benefits can hold up across diverse traffic, weather, and staffing conditions.
key_points: The FAA is taking SMART from a Washington, D.C., pilot to all 22 national airspace centers. It says the system helped reroute 180 flights in the initial rollout, saving about 10 minutes and nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight. The agency hopes those gains translate nationwide, but it has not published independent nationwide performance data.

SMART is a cloud-based decision-support tool, not autopilot. It combines weather, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing data to predict congestion, suggest schedules, identify routes, and sequence arrivals. A team of FAA specialists based in Washington reviews its recommendations before passing them to air traffic control facilities, preserving a human check.

The rollout has a labor support gap. Airline executives publicly favor the expansion, but the controllers’ union says it was not involved in designing or testing the AI system. That dispute matters because controllers must trust and act on recommendations; without union buy-in, adoption and safety reporting could face friction.

Cost and proof remain open questions. The FAA values SMART at $875 million and is promoting time and fuel savings, yet the reported results cover only 180 rerouted flights in one region. Scaling to all 22 centers involves different traffic patterns, weather, and staffing, so benefits and error rates need broader measurement.
report.impact: For the AI industry, SMART is a high-profile test of government AI procurement in a safety-critical domain. It reinforces a human-in-the-loop model: AI predicts and recommends, people validate. Vendors and developers should expect demand for explainable optimization, weather and traffic data integration, and audit trails. For developers, the project highlights opportunities in air traffic management simulation, forecasting, and route optimization, but also strict certification and labor-engagement hurdles. For regular travelers, nationwide use could mean fewer delays and lower fuel burn if the pilot results scale. The bigger risk is trust: if controllers doubt the system or its testing, adoption could stall even when the math looks good.
report.tools: No public open-source version of SMART is available. Readers can follow the FAA’s SMART fact sheet and modernization updates, NASA’s Air Traffic Management–eXploration (ATM-X) research, and EUROCONTROL’s ATM tools. For hands-on exploration, BlueSky is an open-source air traffic simulator, while the OpenSky Network provides flight-tracking data for congestion and routing experiments.
